title: US-Based Software Engineer Arrested for Sending 1,500 Bomb Threat Emails Across India
excerpt: Tamil Nadu's Anti-Terrorism Squad detained Sarath Subramanian Shankar at Chennai airport after a three-year investigation into hoax emails that triggered security alerts at airports, universities and government offices across the country.
body:
• Sarath Subramanian Shankar, a software engineer living in Austin, Texas, was arrested at Chennai International Airport after arriving on an Etihad Airways flight
  • He is accused of sending more than 1,500 hoax bomb threat emails over three years targeting airlines, universities, politicians and law enforcement officials
  • The breakthrough came when the suspect accidentally responded to a threatening email using his personal email account, revealing his identity
  • Mumbai Crime Branch is seeking custody in connection with 32 additional fake bomb threat cases registered in Mumbai between 2024 and 2026

The Tamil Nadu Anti-Terrorism Squad has arrested a US-based Indian software engineer accused of orchestrating one of India's most prolific hoax bomb threat campaigns, sending more than 1,500 threatening emails over a three-year period that repeatedly triggered security alerts across the country.

The accused, Sarath Subramanian Shankar, originally from Ambasamudram in Tamil Nadu's Tirunelveli district, was detained by immigration officials at Chennai International Airport after arriving on an Etihad Airways flight from abroad, according to investigators. He had been living in Austin, Texas, where he worked for a software company.

How One Mistake Unraveled the Operation

Despite using encrypted communication platforms, virtual private networks and dark web infrastructure to conceal his identity, the suspect made a critical error: he accidentally responded to one of his own threatening emails using his personal email account.

That single mistake gave Tamil Nadu's Cyber Crime Wing the breakthrough they needed. Investigators traced the personal email to Shankar and built a case linking him to the campaign.

"Every threat must be treated as credible until verified, requiring the deployment of police personnel, bomb disposal units, fire services and other emergency agencies."

— Future Crime Research Foundation

The investigation was led by Superintendent of Police I. Shanaz during her tenure with the Cyber Crime Wing. After learning Shankar was traveling to India, surveillance was intensified, leading to his arrest at the airport. An ATS team headed by Additional Superintendent of Police Purushothaman took him into custody.

Scale of Disruption

The alleged targets of the threat emails included commercial airlines, educational institutions such as Anna University, politicians, senior police officers, retired Intelligence Bureau officials and other prominent individuals.

Between 2023 and 2025, the anonymous emails forced authorities to conduct repeated emergency security checks at airports, schools and public institutions across India. Every threat ultimately proved to be a hoax, but each required full-scale responses — bomb disposal squads, police teams and other security agencies conducted large-scale searches that consumed substantial public resources and disrupted operations.

The ATS has directly registered 33 cases in Tamil Nadu, while Shankar is linked to more than 100 criminal cases across the state. Mumbai's Crime Branch is now seeking custody in connection with approximately 32 additional fake bomb threat cases registered in the city between 2024 and 2026.

A Growing Digital Threat

Cybersecurity experts from the Future Crime Research Foundation noted that digitally transmitted hoax threats have become an increasingly serious form of cyber-enabled crime. Investigations rely heavily on digital evidence including email headers, IP logs, device forensics and cloud records — and frequently require coordination across international borders.

Investigators are examining Shankar's electronic devices, online activity and digital records to determine whether he acted alone or had assistance. Following interrogation, the accused was handed over to Fort Police Station and remanded to judicial custody.

What's Next

The Tamil Nadu ATS is continuing its investigation to determine the full extent of Shankar's alleged involvement. Multiple states are expected to seek custody as the case broadens. The arrest underscores the growing challenge law enforcement faces in tracing cyber threats that originate from abroad — and the enormous real-world cost of hoax communications that strain emergency response systems nationwide.

nri_angle: The case highlights the legal risks for NRIs whose activities in the US can lead to arrest and prosecution upon returning to India, underscoring the long reach of cross-border cybercrime investigations.
